problem: "Phone chargers, LED drivers, computer supplies and EV chargers use PFC" is an over-generalisation. Ordinary phone chargers (roughly 5 W to 25 W) are below the power and current thresholds of the harmonic standards and almost never have a PFC front end; a student would wrongly conclude his own charger contains a boost PFC stage.
fix: Laptop and desktop supplies, LED drivers above roughly 25 W, and EV chargers and fast chargers above roughly 75 W use PFC to meet harmonic limits and to use the grid better.

problem: The effective input resistance is written "Re = Vrms2/P". With the missing superscript this reads as Vrms times 2, and a student may copy the wrong formula. Elsewhere the chapter uses Unicode superscripts (√2, ²) correctly.
fix: Re = Vrms²/P, where Re is the effective input resistance in Ω, Vrms is the RMS mains voltage in V and P is the input real power in W.

problem: "Below the mains peak the bridge would feed the bus directly" is ambiguous: it can be read as "during the part of the cycle below the peak", which is the opposite of the intended meaning (bus voltage lower than the mains peak).
fix: If the bus voltage were below the mains peak (325.3 V), then near the top of each half-cycle the rectified input would exceed the bus, the bridge diodes would conduct straight into the bus, and the switch would lose control of the inductor current. 400 V keeps the bus above the peak with margin.

problem: "many low-power equipments" is not idiomatic; "equipment" is uncountable in this technical sense and the phrase reads poorly for second-language readers.
fix: IEC 61000-3-2 covers many low-power types of equipment (rated input current up to 16 A per phase); IEEE 519 covers industrial installations.
